title: How’s it going?
description: How are you, or how are things progressing?
details:
Example: Hi, Sam. How’s it going?

Usage: A casual greeting; you can answer Pretty good, thanks.

title: What have you been up to?
description: What have you been doing recently?
details:
Example: I haven’t seen you for ages. What have you been up to?

Usage: A friendly question when catching up with someone.

title: Are you free…?
description: Do you have time to meet or do something?
details:
Example: Are you free on Saturday?

Usage: Add a day or time when arranging plans.

title: Do you fancy…?
description: Would you like something or like to do something?
details:
Example: Do you fancy a coffee?

Usage: Informal British English; use a noun or -ing form: fancy going for a walk?

title: Do you want to come?
description: Would you like to join us?
details:
Example: We’re getting lunch. Do you want to come?

Usage: A straightforward invitation in conversation.

title: Sounds good
description: I like or agree with that suggestion.
details:
Example: Let’s meet at six. Sounds good.

Usage: A casual way to accept a plan.

title: That works for me
description: That arrangement suits my schedule or needs.
details:
Example: How about Tuesday? That works for me.

Usage: Useful when agreeing on a time, place, or plan.

title: Maybe another time
description: I can’t or don’t want to do that now.
details:
Example: Thanks for asking, but maybe another time.

Usage: A gentle refusal; it doesn’t promise a future meeting.

title: Let me know
description: Tell me when you have an answer or more information.
details:
Example: Let me know when you’re free.

Usage: Use when waiting for someone to decide or check something.

title: We should catch up
description: We should meet and share our recent news.
details:
Example: We should catch up over lunch.

Usage: Usually said to someone you already know.

title: Make yourself at home
description: Relax and feel comfortable in my home.
details:
Example: Come in and make yourself at home.

Usage: A friendly welcome to a guest.

title: Help yourself
description: You can take some without asking me again.
details:
Example: There’s cake in the kitchen. Help yourself.

Usage: Use when offering food or something you have made available.

title: It’s on me
description: I’ll pay for this.
details:
Example: Let’s get a coffee. It’s on me.

Usage: An informal offer to pay for the other person too.

title: Thanks for having me
description: Thank you for inviting and welcoming me.
details:
Example: That was lovely. Thanks for having me.

Usage: Useful when leaving someone’s home after a visit or meal.

title: It was nice seeing you
description: I enjoyed spending time with you.
details:
Example: It was nice seeing you. Let’s do it again.

Usage: A friendly goodbye after meeting someone you know.

title: Say hi to…
description: Please pass on my friendly greeting.
details:
Example: Say hi to your sister for me.

Usage: A casual alternative to sending someone your regards.

title: Keep in touch
description: Let’s continue contacting each other.
details:
Example: Good luck with the move. Keep in touch.

Usage: Useful when saying goodbye to someone you may not see soon.

title: Sorry, I didn’t mean that
description: What I said wasn’t what I intended.
details:
Example: Sorry, I didn’t mean that. I’m just tired.

Usage: Use to take back hurtful or inaccurate words; explain or apologise properly if needed.

title: Are you okay?
description: Is something wrong, or do you need help?
details:
Example: You seem quiet. Are you okay?

Usage: Your tone should show care when checking how someone feels.

title: I’m here if you need me
description: You can ask me for support.
details:
Example: That sounds tough. I’m here if you need me.

Usage: A reassuring offer; leave the person room to decide whether to talk.
